## Utilitarian analysis

A mandatory universal genetic-screening program could be justified, on utilitarian grounds, if it substantially reduces suffering and premature death. Early identification of severe, treatable diseases may allow prompt interventions, better public-health planning, and lower long-term medical costs. Universal coverage also avoids inequalities created when only affluent families can access predictive screening.

The same lens also counts harms: false positives may cause anxiety and unnecessary treatment; false negatives may create misplaced reassurance; data breaches could expose lifelong sensitive information; and inaccurate risk prediction could stigmatize children before they have symptoms. A utilitarian judgment would depend on empirical balances: disease severity, test accuracy, treatment effectiveness, privacy safeguards, and social trust.

## Deontological analysis

From a deontological perspective, mandatory screening raises concerns about autonomy, consent, and treating newborns or families as instruments of public-health optimization. Even beneficial programs can be morally constrained if they override parental decision-making, bodily integrity, or a child’s future right not to know certain genetic information.

However, deontological duties can also support screening: governments and clinicians may have duties to prevent serious avoidable harm, protect children who cannot consent, and provide equal access to lifesaving care.

## Edge cases

One edge case is a condition that is predictable but untreatable: knowing may burden the family without medical benefit. Another is a genetic marker correlated with disease only in some ancestries, risking unequal accuracy and discriminatory classification. A further case is secondary findings about parents or relatives who did not consent. A neutral ethical assessment must therefore weigh benefits, rights, accuracy, coercion, and governance rather than treating screening as categorically good or bad.
